'''Linn Frederick Mollenauer''' (1937–2021) was an American physicist who worked on [[quantum optics]], including the study of [[solitons]] in [[fiber optics]].<ref name="NYTObit">{{cite web|title=LINN F. MOLLINAUER 1937 - 2021|publisher=Physics Department at the University of California at Berkeley|url=https://physics.berkeley.edu/news-events/news/20211115/linn-f-mollinauer-1937-2021|access-date=30 December 2021}}</ref>

Mollenauer was born on 6 January 1937.<ref name="NYTObit"/> He studied at Cornell University, receiving his doctorate in physics from Stanford University in 1965.<ref name="NYTObit"/> He taught for seven years at Berkeley, before embarking on a research career at [[Bell Labs]] from 1972.<ref name="NYTObit"/>

A key advance was in February 1993, when Mollenauer succeeded in transmitting "10 billion bits per second through 20,000 kilometres of fibers with a simple soliton system".<ref>{{cite book|last=Hechdt|first=Jeff|title=City of Light: The Story of Fiber Optics|year=2004|page=276}}</ref>

In 1982, he received the [[R. W. Wood Prize]].<ref name="OPTICA">{{cite web|title=Linn F. Mollenauer|publisher=OPTICA|url=https://www.optica.org/en-us/history/biographies/bios/linn_f_mollenauer/|access-date=30 December 2021}}</ref> In 1986, Mollenauer was awarded the [[Stuart Ballantine Medal]].<ref>{{cite web|title=LINN F. MOLLENAUER|publisher=The Franklin Institute|url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/linn-f-mollenauer|access-date=30 December 2021}}</ref> Mollenauer was one of the recipients of the 1991 [[Rank Prizes|Rank Prize in Optoelectronics]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Optoelectronics winners|publisher=Rank Prize|url=https://www.rankprize.org/prize/optoelectronics/winners/|access-date=30 December 2021}}</ref> He received the [[Charles Hard Townes Award]] in 1997.<ref name="OPTICA"/> In 2001, he was the recipient of the Quantum Electronics Award of the [[IEEE Photonics Society]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Quantum Electronics Award Winners|publisher=IEEE Photonics Society|url=https://www.photonicssociety.org/awards/quantum-electronics-award/quantum-electronics-award-award-winners|access-date=30 December 2021|archive-date=5 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181005153858/https://www.photonicssociety.org/awards/quantum-electronics-award/quantum-electronics-award-award-winners|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dr. Linn F. Mollenauer|publisher=National Academy of Engineering|url=https://www.nae.edu/19579/19581/20412/29989/Dr-Linn-F-Mollenauer|access-date=30 December 2021}}</ref> He was elected a Fellow of [[Bell Labs]] in 2001.<ref name="NYTObit"/> He was also a fellow of the [[Optica (society)|Optical Society of America]].<ref name="OPTICA"/>

Mollenauer was co-author with [[James P. Gordon]] of the work ''Solitons in Optical Fibers: Fundamentals and Applications'' (2006) <ref>{{cite web|title=Solitons in Optical Fibers: Fundamentals and Applications|publisher=Elsevier|url=https://www.elsevier.com/books/solitons-in-optical-fibers/mollenauer/978-0-12-504190-4|access-date=30 December 2021}}</ref>

Mollenauer died on 28 July 2021.<ref name="NYTObit"/>
